query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-sintering atomic layer deposition (ALD) of a nanometer‐scale copper wetting layer on tungsten surfaces will enhance Cu infiltration and interparticle bonding in W–Cu composites, thereby minimizing phase separation and void formation while preserving mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite prepared from either discrete W particles or connected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix using conventional sintering or casting methods; the untreated baseline shows voids and phase separation at the W–Cu interface.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (a few nanometers) ALD Cu (or Cu-alloy) coating selectively onto the surfaces of tungsten prior to Cu matrix incorporation and sintering.
generation.conditions: Fabrication under processing temperatures well below the melting point of W and within typical ALD and sintering regimes (sub-1000 °C), with subsequent service conditions mimicking fusion-reactor joint environments including high-temperature cycling and irradiation.
generation.structural_mediator: The ALD coating promotes atomic interdiffusion and a uniform, conformal Cu–W interface, thereby reducing interfacial energy barriers and eliminating nucleation sites for voids during sintering.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced wettability provided by the ALD layer facilitates uniform Cu infiltration into the W scaffold, reducing the likelihood of phase separation and void formation. This improved bonding at the interface maintains continuous thermal pathways and mechanical integrity, even under irradiation conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional processing (e.g., spark plasma sintering or vapor-coated W powders), the ALD-treated W–Cu composites will exhibit a significantly reduced void fraction (detectable by micro-CT and microscopy), improved interfacial thermal conductance, and preserved mechanical durability during simulated irradiation tests.
generation.baseline: Existing fabrication techniques such as spark-plasma sintering and vapor-coated W powder sintering, which often leave residual interfacial voids or phase-separated regions that impair thermal transport and durability under irradiation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to composites where W exists as particles or connected regions within a Cu matrix, processed within temperature regimes conducive to ALD and sintering (e.g., below 1000 °C) and effective under irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactor joints.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal ALD coating thickness and its long-term stability under high neutron flux and thermal cycling require further quantification. Additionally, variations in ALD precursor chemistry may alter the interfacial structure in ways that need systematic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites under identical sintering conditions: one set with pre-deposited ALD Cu (or Cu-alloy) coatings on W and one set without any surface treatment. Characterize the interfacial microstructure using high-resolution SEM/TEM and micro-CT to quantify void formation, measure thermal conductivity across the interface, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and fatigue) before and after simulated irradiation cycles.
measurements: Void fraction and interfacial quality via micro-CT and SEM/TEM imaging
Thermal conductivity measurements across the W–Cu interface
Mechanical durability tests (tensile strength, fatigue resistance) pre- and post-irradiation simulation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-treated composites do not show a statistically significant (>20%) improvement in interfacial integrity, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability relative to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is rejected.
